When I was nine, there was a story at our school that the old water tank behind the playground was haunted.
First, one girl said her brother heard footsteps there. I laughed. Then Noor told me three more people had heard it. Then my whole bench was talking about it. By Friday, even the older kids said it.
Each time I heard it, it felt a little more real. By the end of the week, I wouldn't go near the tank, even to fetch a ball. My heart pounded if I even looked at it.
Years later I realised nobody had ever seen anything. One story just got said so many times that it started to feel like a fact.
Jyoti, I sometimes tell myself now, count how many people actually saw it.

Class 4 teacher's note, Monday. From Manjula, class teacher.
This week a story spread that the old neem tree near the gate is haunted. On Monday one child said it. By Wednesday, I heard it from almost every group.
Samir usually plays under that tree. On Wednesday, he wouldn't go near it. He told me, "Ma'am, everyone says a ghost lives there. It must be true if so many people say it." His hands were cold.
I asked him who had actually seen something. He counted. "Nobody. They just heard."
What I did next: I took the class out at lunch and we all sat under the neem and ate. I asked each child to say if they'd seen anything themselves. Nobody had. Samir climbed back onto his favourite root.

qa.a: He felt frightened, with cold hands, because hearing the story from so many people made it seem true.

qa.a: It let the children check for themselves and count who had really seen something, so the story stopped growing.

qa.a: They probably felt nervous at first, then relieved and a little silly when nobody had seen anything.
